The shop appeared between the pharmacy and the laundromat on a Tuesday, which was inconvenient, because I had walked that stretch of pavement every morning for eleven years and preferred not to discover that the world had been keeping spare rooms.

Its window contained a chair, a green apple, and a handwritten sign:

**MINOR LOSSES RECOVERED.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**No people. No pets. No exceptions.**

I went in because of a blue button.

It had fallen from my father’s coat the winter before he died. I remembered hearing it strike the kitchen floor, remembered thinking I would pick it up after I finished washing the cup in my hand. By the time I set down the cup, I had forgotten.

This was nineteen years ago. I had no practical use for the button. The coat was gone.

A woman behind the counter was repairing an umbrella with a needle threaded through rain.

“Keys?” she asked.

“A button.”

“Buttons are easy.”

“It’s been a long time.”

“That generally isn’t the difficulty.”

She put the umbrella aside. A few drops fell upward.

“Describe it.”

“Blue. Dark blue. Four holes. A scratch along one edge.”

“Material?”

“I don’t know.”

“Most people don’t.”

She opened a drawer and took out a small white dish. In it lay the button.

I recognized the scratch. For a moment, I also recognized the kitchen: the damp windows, the cup warming my fingers, my father at the table struggling out of his coat.

“What does it cost?”

“What were you doing when you lost it?”

“Washing a cup.”

“Then a cup will do.”

“There’s no cup here.”

“Bring one tomorrow.”

I took the button home.

It was lighter than I remembered.

***

The next morning I brought a yellow mug from the back of my cupboard. The woman turned it over, checked the base, and nodded.

I asked whether she could recover other things.

“Sometimes.”

“A conversation?”

“Words, occasionally. Not conversations.”

“An opportunity?”

“No.”

“A feeling?”

She looked up sharply.

“What feeling?”

I hadn’t expected to be asked. Outside, a bus sighed at the curb.

“Never mind.”

She took the mug to a shelf already crowded with cups. One had a broken handle; another was so small it might have belonged to a doll.

“People usually come back three times,” she said.

“What happens the third time?”

“They ask for something I can’t give them.”

***

On my second visit, I asked for six minutes.

“When?”

“June. About twenty years ago. Maybe twenty-one.”

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

She waited.

I had been sitting on a wall behind a supermarket with a woman named Elise. We were sharing a carton of strawberries we hadn’t paid for yet. It was hot, and the bricks were warm through my shirt.

There had been six minutes—perhaps five, perhaps eight—when I was not thinking about what came next. Not work. Not whether Elise liked me as much as I liked her. Not the unopened envelope on the table at home.

A delivery truck was backing toward the loading dock. Elise had a strawberry seed stuck to her wrist. She was telling me about something her brother had done, and I was laughing too hard to hear the end.

The shopkeeper listened without touching anything.

“You can’t take those away with you,” she said.

“I don’t need to.”

She went through a curtain behind the counter and returned carrying a shallow wooden box.

“Sit down.”

The chair from the window was beside me now. I sat.

She opened the lid.

I had expected light, or a scent, or some other trick I could recognize as a trick.

Instead, my shoulders dropped. The chair was comfortable. There was no particular reason to speak.

The woman continued repairing her umbrella.

After a while, she closed the box.

“How long?” I asked.

“Six minutes.”

I rubbed my palms against my knees. I wanted her to open it again, but I was embarrassed to ask.

“What do I owe you?”

“An afternoon.”

“Which one?”

“One you haven’t made plans for.”

I agreed before asking how she would collect it.

***

On my third visit, I brought nothing.

The shopkeeper was eating the green apple.

“I wondered when you’d come,” she said.

“I want the last time I spoke to my father.”

“No people.”

“Not him. The call.”

“Tell me.”

He had called to ask whether I knew where his spare glasses were. I was at work. Someone stood beside my desk, waiting for me to finish.

I told him to check the drawer by the stove.

He asked how I was.

“Fine,” I said. “Busy.”

“All right. I’ll let you go.”

Those were his last words to me.

“I want to answer differently.”

“You can’t.”

“I could have talked for another minute.”

“Yes.”

I disliked her for agreeing.

She put the apple down.

“What did you say after that?”

“After what?”

“After he said he’d let you go.”

I tried to remember the phone in my hand, the person beside my desk. For years, I had stopped at my father’s words.

“I said, ‘Talk to you Sunday.’”

“And?”

“He said, ‘Right you are.’”

I sat down without being asked.

The woman gave me a clean handkerchief from beneath the counter. I didn’t use it, but held it until she needed to close.

***

The shop was gone the next morning.

Between the pharmacy and the laundromat stood a narrow brick wall, darkened near the pavement. I ran my fingers along the mortar.

That Saturday, I meant to clear out a cupboard. Instead, I fell asleep on the sofa after lunch and woke when it was nearly dark. I couldn’t account for the hours.

In my pocket was the blue button.

I keep it in the drawer by the stove. Sometimes, looking for batteries or a rubber band, I come across it. I turn it over, feel the scratch with my thumb, and put it back.
